rows: roy-two-copyrights
Every recorded song holds two separate copyrights
The song (music and lyrics) and the recording of it are two works, each with its own rights and its own income.
roy-term-musical-work
Musical work (the song)
The composition: the music plus any words that go with it. Its authors are the people who wrote the music and lyrics, unless it was made for hire.
roy-term-sound-recording
Sound recording (the master)
A work made by fixing a series of sounds, such as a recorded performance. In US law it excludes sounds that accompany a film or other audiovisual work.
roy-who-owns-recording
A recording's authors: the performer and producer, unless made for hire
The Copyright Office names the featured performer and the producer as authors of a sound recording. For a work made for hire, the employer or hiring party is the author.
roy-mistake-one-registration
Mistake: registering the song and assuming the recording is covered
A registration for a song covers its music and lyrics, not the recorded performance. Recordings are normally registered on their own.
roy-registration-optional
Copyright protection starts on creation; registration is a separate step
A US sound recording made since 1978 is protected from the moment it is fixed. Registering with the Copyright Office is a separate step with its own form, fee and deposit.
roy-table-streams-us
Income streams and who collects each in the US
A song and a recording earn through different rights, and different bodies collect them. This table covers the main US routes.
roy-note-mechanical-vs-performance
Mechanical and performance royalties pay for different uses
A mechanical royalty pays for making copies of a song, and a performance royalty pays when it is performed or communicated to the public.
roy-term-mechanical
Mechanical right
The right to record a song and to make copies of that recording and distribute them. In the US, streaming and download services get it for songs through the MLC's blanket licence.
roy-term-performing-right
Performing right
The right to perform a song publicly, or to authorise others to. US law counts a performance as public where the public can attend, or when it is transmitted to the public.
roy-no-us-performance-right-recording
US recordings have no general public performance right
A US sound recording owner has a performance right only for digital audio transmissions, not the broader right that song owners hold.
roy-sync
Sync licences need permission for the song and for the recording
Putting music in a film, ad or game is licensed by deal. In practice, using an existing recording means clearing both the song and the recording.
roy-print-lyrics
Printed music and lyrics are another reproduction use
Printed sheet music counts as a reproduction of the song. Lyrics are part of the song, so using them is also a use of the song.
roy-term-neighbouring
Neighbouring (related) rights

Rights that performers, record producers and broadcasters hold, separate from the copyright in the song. Also called related rights. Societies in many countries manage them for broadcasts and public play of recordings.
roy-number-cisac-digital
Digital was 42% of CISAC collections, all repertoires, in 2025
Digital was EUR 6.57 bn, up 27.9% on 2024, partly because The MLC reported for the first time. Without The MLC, digital grew 11.6%.
42.4 percent of EUR 15.5 bn, all repertoires, 2025
roy-mlc
The MLC collects US digital mechanicals for songs
The MLC collects mechanical royalties from eligible US streaming and download services under the blanket licence, then pays the song's owners.
roy-pros
Performing rights societies collect for public performance of songs
In the US, a performing rights society licenses public performance of songs for their owners. The statute names ASCAP, BMI and SESAC; Songview also lists GMR.
roy-soundexchange
SoundExchange collects digital performance money for recordings
SoundExchange pays recording owners and artists for digital play on non-interactive services, but only those who have registered with it.
roy-writer-publisher-share
A song's income divides into a writer share and a publisher share
Where a song has a publisher, a society divides its income between the writer and the publisher, by their contract, the society's rules, or both.
roy-term-writer-share
Writer's share and publisher's share
Common industry names for the part of a song's income that goes to its writers and the part that goes to its publishers. See the note on how societies divide it.
roy-publisher
A publisher licenses songs and pays advances
A music publisher gets the right to license a writer's songs, collects the income, and often pays an advance that is later recovered from royalties.
roy-term-administrator
Publishing administrator
Industry name for a company that registers songs, collects their income and keeps the records on an owner's behalf, without becoming the owner. Terms vary by contract.
roy-table-digital-performance-split
Statutory digital performance split for recordings, as the law states it
Section 114(g)(2) sets how the designated collective divides statutory licence money for digital transmission of recordings, after any costs it deducts. Other income is not covered.
roy-checklist-registrations
Registrations for a songwriter and for an artist
Each kind of money has its own register. Tick what applies to you and check it separately; one registration does not cover another.
roy-step-register-song
Register a song before it earns
Register each new song with your performing rights society and with the MLC, then check that every register shows the same details.
roy-step-register-recording
Register the recording when it is released
Register with SoundExchange, make sure the recording has an ISRC, and check it is linked to the song so the song's owners are paid.
roy-term-isrc
ISRC code
International Standard Recording Code: a 12-character identifier for one recording, made of a rightsholder code, a year and a five-digit number.
roy-term-iswc
ISWC code
International Standard Musical Work Code: a number that identifies a song and links it to its rights holders in the society systems.
roy-later-topics
Pre-1972 recordings and producer letters of direction have their own rules
Title II of the Music Modernization Act gives federal remedies to recordings fixed before 15 February 1972. Title III lets producers, mixers and engineers be paid by letter of direction.
roy-table-international
Who collects what in the UK, Canada and Germany
A basic map, limited to bodies whose pages were read for this guide. Other countries and rights are not shown, and rules differ by body.
roy-reciprocal
Societies work abroad through reciprocal agreements
A society licenses mainly at home. To be paid abroad, societies appoint each other, so foreign income reaches you through your own society.
roy-neighbouring-abroad
Outside the US, recordings can earn neighbouring rights money
In the UK and Canada, PPL and Re:Sound deal with money for recordings on behalf of performers and recording owners. It is a separate account from songwriter income.
roy-uk-ppl
PPL divides UK recording money between rightsholders and performers
For UK public play and broadcasts, PPL matches reported use against its database of over 28 million recordings and, after costs, pays half to rightsholders and half to qualifying performers.
roy-flow-song
How money moves from a stream to a songwriter
A service reports plays and pays a collector, which matches them to registered songs and pays the owners on file. A writer may be paid by the collector directly or through a publisher.
roy-flow-recording
How money moves from a stream to an artist
Statutory digital performance money goes through SoundExchange and is split by law. Other recording income reaches the artist through the recording owner, as the contract says.
roy-w8ben
Form W-8 BEN: a form non-US payees may be asked to give
The IRS says a foreign person who is the "beneficial owner of an amount subject to withholding" gives this form to whoever withholds the tax or makes the payment.
pro-note-public-performance-right
US law gives song owners the exclusive right to perform in public
Section 106(4) gives the owner of a musical work the exclusive right to perform it publicly, live or by transmission. A PRO licenses that right for its members.
pro-term-pro
Performing rights organisation (PRO)
A body that licenses public performance of non-dramatic musical works for their owners. US law calls it a performing rights society.
pro-term-blanket-license
Blanket licence (performing right)
One licence that lets a user perform any work in a society's repertoire, including foreign works it represents under reciprocal deals, with no song-by-song clearance.
pro-note-why-collective
Collective licensing exists because song-by-song deals do not scale
A PRO pools many owners' rights so a user can cover many songs with one licence, and a writer does not chase every bar, station and service alone.
pro-note-venue-responsible
GMR says the venue, not the performer, must hold the licence
GMR states that the operator of a venue, not the musicians or DJs playing there, is responsible for licensing the music performed on its premises.
pro-note-licences-separate
A licence from one US PRO does not cover another PRO's songs
GMR says a venue licensed by ASCAP, BMI or SESAC still needs a GMR licence to play GMR writers' music, and the reverse also holds.
pro-note-assignment
Many societies take your performing right, not just a mandate to collect
In many English-speaking countries a society takes over ownership of the performing right outright, so it holds that right and can enforce it.
pro-table-us-pros
ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR compared on facts the sources state
ASCAP and BMI are bound by DOJ consent decrees and SESAC and GMR are not. The scale figures are each PRO's own, so treat them as claims.
pro-note-gmr-invitation
GMR describes its client base as invitation-only
GMR describes a client base chosen by invitation.
pro-number-market-share
In 2021 the DOJ put ASCAP and BMI at about 90 percent of performance licensing
The DOJ's January 2021 figure for the two decree-bound PROs' combined share of the US market. It also noted more PROs had entered since. Newer figures were not checked.
90 percent of US public performance licensing, ASCAP and BMI
pro-note-consent-decrees
The ASCAP and BMI consent decrees shape what each can do
The decrees bar exclusive licensing, let members license their works directly, and require ASCAP and BMI to accept qualifying members.
pro-note-decrees-only-two
SESAC and GMR are not bound by the consent decrees
The DOJ notes that the two decrees bind only ASCAP and BMI, so other PROs work without those limits. Terms can differ.
pro-note-doj-2021-closing
In January 2021 the DOJ closed its review of the decrees and proposed no changes
The DOJ closed its review of the ASCAP and BMI decrees on 15 January 2021, proposed no changes, and called for a fresh review every five years.
pro-note-fractional-licensing
Under fractional licensing, each PRO licenses only its own share of a song
A user then needs a licence from every PRO with a share of the song, or from the owners directly. The Second Circuit held that BMI's decree permits this.
pro-note-partial-withdrawal
As of 2021, publishers could not pull only streaming rights from ASCAP or BMI
Partial withdrawal would let an owner keep digital services out of a PRO licence. The DOJ says a 2013 attempt to read the decrees that way failed.
pro-note-ascap-performance-only
ASCAP's decree limits it to performance rights
The DOJ says ASCAP's decree bars licensing anything but performance rights, while BMI's decree is silent on other rights.
pro-note-mma-rate-court
The Music Modernization Act changed how ASCAP and BMI rate disputes are heard
Per the DOJ, since the Act, ASCAP and BMI rate disputes go to one of several judges in the Southern District of New York, not the judge who oversees the decree.
pro-note-usco-inquiry
The Copyright Office ran a 2025 inquiry into PROs and sent Congress a summary
Congress asked the Office to look at the rise in PRO numbers and how PROs distribute. The Office's 20 November 2025 letter made no new policy recommendations.
pro-note-pro-transparency
The Copyright Office says not every PRO discloses what it licenses or how it pays
The Office notes that more PROs may weaken licensing efficiency and that some do not publish full repertoire or distribution policies.
pro-note-songview
Songview was built so licensees can see each song's owners and shares
The DOJ says ASCAP and BMI launched Songview in December 2020 as an authoritative listing of who owns each song in their repertories and in what shares.
pro-mistake-publisher-share
Registering the writer side and never checking who holds the publisher share
Many songs have at least a writer and a publisher. If the publisher side of a registration is empty or wrong, the song may not pay as you expect.
pro-mistake-live-sets
Not reporting live sets can leave live performances unpaid
A society cannot pay for a use it does not know about. For many live shows the writer reports the set, so keep dates and set lists.
pro-note-socan-join
SOCAN membership has no fee for writers and a five-work test for publishers
A composer, songwriter, producer or lyricist can join SOCAN free if a work is published, recorded or performed where SOCAN licenses it. Publishers need five qualifying works.
pro-note-gema-join
GEMA charges an admission fee and a yearly fee, and waives the first for younger creators
A creator pays EUR 90 plus VAT to join and EUR 50 a year. Creators who turn 30 or younger in the year they apply pay no admission fee.
pro-table-join
Joining terms at SOCAN, GEMA and GMR as their pages state them
Eligibility and cost differ sharply: SOCAN is free to writers, GEMA charges fees, and GMR admits clients by invitation.
pro-term-cue-sheet
Cue sheet
A list of the music in a TV or film programme, with each work and use, sent to a society so it can pay the writers and publishers.
pro-note-socan-schedule
SOCAN pays performing-right royalties on set dates, with cut-offs before each
SOCAN's 2026 schedule lists performing-right payments on 15 May, 14 August and 13 November, each with cut-offs for cue sheets and agreements.
pro-note-distribution-methods
Societies may pay from samples or proxy data when counting every play is impractical
WIPO says ideal pay-per-play is not always practical, so societies may pay from a sample of uses or from a proxy source such as radio data.
pro-note-gema-distribution
GEMA states it is non-profit and pays by its members' distribution plan
GEMA says its only deductions are administration costs and money for members' social and cultural support, and distribution follows its plan.
pro-note-foreign-live
Live shows abroad are licensed by the local society, so tell your own society
A venue abroad deals with its local society, which licenses foreign repertoire by reciprocal agreement. Your own society needs your dates to follow up.
pro-checklist-setup
Setting up for performance royalties
A short order of work: pick a society, register each work with its shares, then keep records of live and screen uses.
mech-compulsory-license-term
Compulsory (mechanical) license

A US legal route to record and distribute your own version of a song once recordings of it have been released in the US with the owner's permission. You must meet the conditions and pay the statutory rate.
mech-phonorecord-term
Phonorecord and digital phonorecord delivery (DPD)

A phonorecord is an object that holds recorded sound, such as vinyl or a CD. A DPD is a digital transmission that leaves the recipient with a specific copy: a permanent or limited download, or an on-demand stream.
mech-noi-term
Notice of intention (NOI)
The notice a person serves on a song's copyright owner, or files with the Copyright Office when the owner cannot be found in its records, to use the compulsory license for physical copies.
mech-blanket-license-term
Blanket license (digital)
Since 1 January 2021, a qualifying digital service can get one license through the MLC that covers every song open to the compulsory license, in place of song-by-song notices.
mech-mistake-recording-not-covered
Treating a mechanical license as permission to use someone's recording
Section 115 covers the song only. Copying another person's recording needs separate permission from whoever owns that recording.
mech-step-noi-physical
Serve the notice before you distribute physical copies
For a compulsory license on vinyl or CDs, serve an NOI on the owner before, or within 30 days after, making copies, and always before distributing any.
mech-digital-via-mlc
Digital mechanicals now run through the MLC, physical ones still use NOIs
Since 2021 a digital service licenses US mechanicals from the MLC under a blanket license. Physical copies still use the song-by-song notice route.
mech-rate-physical-2026
Physical and download mechanical rate per work, 2026
The 2026 per-song rate, unless the per-minute rate of 2.52 cents is larger. The notice applies it from 1 January to 31 December 2026.
13.1 cents per work, physical and downloads, 2026
mech-rate-permin-2026
Per-minute alternative for long tracks, 2026
Applies to a work when it comes out larger than the 13.1 cent flat rate. Each started minute counts as a minute.
2.52 cents per minute or fraction, 2026
mech-rate-ringtone
Ringtone mechanical rate
The fixed ringtone rate in 37 CFR 385.11(b) on the retrieval date. It is not part of the yearly cost-of-living adjustment.
24 cents per ringtone, per work
mech-note-long-tracks
Past five minutes, the per-minute rate sets the price of a copy
For copies and downloads the rate is the larger of a flat amount and a per-minute amount, so a track over five minutes costs more per copy than a shorter one.
mech-note-cola
The physical and download rate is adjusted every January for inflation
The Judges publish a cost-of-living notice at least 25 days before 1 January. It indexes base rates of 12 cents and 2.31 cents to the CPI-U published in November 2022.
mech-mistake-streaming-per-stream
Reading 13.1 cents as what a stream pays
The 13.1 cent figure is for physical copies and downloads. Streaming mechanicals come from a pool formula, not a fixed amount per play.
mech-rate-streaming-pct-2026
Streaming revenue percentage for 2026
Table 1 in 37 CFR 385.21: the revenue prong for 2026, which is compared with a content-cost prong. The same table gives 15.35 for 2027.
15.3 % of service revenue, 2026 (first prong)
mech-table-streaming-prongs
Streaming content-cost prongs by type of offering
The second prong of the streaming formula depends on the offering. TCC is the service's expensed cost of the rights it takes for streams and limited downloads.
mech-note-streaming-steps
Streaming mechanicals are worked out in four steps from a pool
Take the greater of the revenue and content-cost prongs, subtract performance royalties, apply any floor, then split the pool across plays.
mech-mlc-term
The MLC (Mechanical Licensing Collective)

The non-profit the Copyright Office designated on 8 July 2019 to run the blanket license: it collects digital mechanicals, matches them to songs and owners, distributes them, and keeps the public database.
mech-dlc-term
The DLC (Digital Licensee Coordinator)

The non-profit that represents licensed digital services. It names a non-voting member of the MLC board and can take part in Copyright Royalty Board proceedings that set the assessment funding the MLC.
mech-note-mlc-funding
The MLC does not take a fee from mechanical royalties
The MLC says digital services fund its operating budget and that it takes no fees out of the mechanical royalties it pays.
mech-table-mlc-snapshots
MLC scale figures differ by date, so quote the date
The MLC's own pages give different totals because they were written at different times. Its tools page still says 55 million works. Cite the source and date with any figure.
mech-mistake-copyright-not-mlc
Assuming a copyright registration puts your song in the MLC
A Copyright Office registration and an MLC registration are different. You, or your publisher or administrator, need the MLC record to be paid blanket-license digital mechanicals.
mech-step-search-first
Search the public database before you register a song
Use the MLC's Public Work Search to see if the song exists and who is credited. Search by title, ISWC, MLC or HFA song code, writer or publisher.
mech-step-claim-register
Claim your share or register the work, then add your details
Join the MLC, use the Claiming Tool for songs that exist, use the Works Registration Tools for songs that do not, and keep banking and tax details current.
mech-step-match-recordings
Check the Matching Tool for recordings not yet tied to your songs
Unmatched recordings can earn royalties the MLC holds. Propose matches in the Matching Tool, and look again, as new usage data arrives continuously.
mech-checklist-get-paid
Getting paid digital mechanicals by the MLC: a checklist
A short order of work for a writer or admin. It follows what the MLC says each tool does.
mech-overclaim-term
Overclaim
A song where the shares claimed by all members together come to more than 100 percent. The MLC's Overclaims Tool lets owners amend or give up shares and upload documents while it is resolved.
mech-note-database-limits
The MLC database is free to search, but its ownership data can be wrong or partial
Public search is free by law, and bulk and API access must be offered too. The MLC warns that listed ownership may be incomplete or out of date.
mech-unclaimed-accrued-term
Unclaimed accrued royalties
Money the MLC has collected but still cannot match to an owner or pay out when the legal minimum holding period ends. The MLC counts both unmatched and unclaimed amounts in it.
mech-market-share-term
Market-share distribution
How the statute says remaining unclaimed accrued royalties are paid: to identified owners in proportion to their relative market shares in the usage reports, with a share passed on to songwriters.
mech-note-april-2027
April 2027 is when market-share distributions begin, one month at a time
The MLC plans to start in April 2027 with January 2021 usage, then take one more month of usage each month. It is a start date, not a cut-off.
mech-note-claim-early
Claiming before a month's royalties are distributed gets you the accrued amount
If an owner is found before the accrued royalties are included in a market-share distribution, the MLC pays them to that owner with interest.
mech-note-holding-period
The MLC must hold unmatched royalties for at least three years first
The statute sets a three-year minimum hold, in an interest-bearing account, before unmatched money can go into a market-share distribution.
mech-note-songwriter-share
Publishers must pass a share of unclaimed distributions to songwriters
Owners who receive an unclaimed distribution must pay or credit songwriters by reported usage, and never under half of what the owner receives for that songwriter's works.
mech-number-historical-transferred
Historical unmatched royalties that services transferred to the MLC
Twenty-one services transferred money for 2007 to 2020 use. The first total was about $427 million, adjusted down after final rates.
397 million USD, approx., after Phono III adjustments
mech-number-historical-distributed
Historical royalties distributed by September 2026
The MLC reports it has distributed nearly this much, which it says is over 60 percent of the historical unmatched total.
239 million USD, approx., historical royalties
mech-note-historical
Historical royalties cover 2007 to 2020 and are separate from blanket royalties
Services handed over unmatched money for 2007 to 2020 streams in early 2021. The MLC began paying matched amounts in 2022 and has not started market-share distributions for them.
mech-table-money-pools
Three pools of MLC money and where each stands
The MLC separates ongoing blanket royalties, historical unmatched royalties and the remainder it will pay by market share.
mech-note-study-2021
The Copyright Office recommended holding unclaimed money longer than the minimum
The Office's July 2021 report recommends no first distribution until at least five years after claiming was fully available. The MMA requires the MLC to give the report substantial weight.
mech-note-statement-layouts
MLC statements come in two layouts: by recording or by work
Royalty Detail shows rows per sound recording from the services' reports. Work Summary rolls the same money up per musical work. Both are .tsv files.
mech-note-dsp-audits
The MLC can audit digital services, at most once in any three calendar years
An audit covers up to three full calendar years, starts with a notice filed at the Copyright Office, and is done by an independent qualified auditor.
mech-number-audit-notices
Services sent MLC audit notice letters for 2021 to 2023
The MLC preserved audit rights for 1 January 2021 to 31 December 2023. The page lists the services but gives no results.
49 DSPs listed on notice letters dated 10 January 2024
mech-table-rate-periods
The rate periods referred to in MLC and CRB documents
Proceedings are named Phonorecords I to V. The years below are the ones the cited pages state.
mech-note-phono-v
Phonorecords V is open, and a partial settlement on physical rates is under review
The 2028 to 2032 proceeding is in discovery. A partial settlement on physical copies, downloads, ringtones and bundles was proposed in June 2026; the Judges have split it off and paused it.
nbr-note-two-routes
Non-interactive services license by statute; interactive services license from the owner
Section 114 gives non-interactive digital services a statutory licence at rates the Judges set. An interactive service needs a licence from the recording owner.
nbr-mistake-radio-pays
Mistake: treating a radio station's online stream like its broadcast
Over-the-air play on a US AM or FM station is exempt from the recording's digital performance right. A broadcaster's stream under the statutory licence pays per play.
nbr-note-sx-collective
The Judges name the collective for the statutory licence, and for now it is SoundExchange
The Judges designate the collective, and the 2026 commercial broadcaster rule names SoundExchange for the current rate period. Services pay it and send play reports.
nbr-term-roles
Artist, Performer and Sound Recording Owner (SoundExchange's terms)

SoundExchange uses Artist for the name on the release, Performer for each person who makes up that Artist, and Sound Recording Owner for whoever owns the master, which is separate from owning the song.
nbr-note-collab-split
A "featuring" credit splits the featured share equally, and each artist signs a letter
SoundExchange treats "Artist A featuring Artist B" as a collaboration and divides the featured-artist share 50/50, unless both artists tell it another split.
nbr-term-featured
Featured and non-featured performers
A featured artist is the person or group most prominent on a track. Non-featured performers, such as session musicians and backing singers, are paid through a separate route.
nbr-note-nonfeatured
Non-featured musicians and vocalists are paid through funds, not directly by SoundExchange
Session musicians and backing vocalists get their statutory share through two escrow funds, not from SoundExchange, whether or not they belong to a union.
nbr-step-lod
A letter of direction needs a signed form, a repertoire chart and a percentage
SoundExchange asks for a signed form, a chart of the tracks covered with a percentage for each, and proof of any electronic signature. Allow at least two weeks.
nbr-note-pre1972-licence
Pre-1972 recordings are partly inside federal law, including the statutory licences
The Copyright Office says Title II of the Music Modernization Act brought recordings fixed before 15 February 1972 partly into federal law, with remedies and a licensing regime.
nbr-table-pre1972-terms
How long federal remedies run for pre-1972 recordings
The Office says remedies last 95 years from the year of first publication, plus an additional period that depends on when the recording was first published.
nbr-note-pre1972-schedule
Pre-1972 owners usually file a schedule first, and remedies start 90 days after indexing
To recover statutory damages or attorneys' fees for a pre-1972 recording, owners must typically file a schedule with the Copyright Office. Only later uses count.
nbr-number-broadcasters-2026
Commercial broadcasters' nonsubscription streaming rate per performance, 2026
Web VI rate for a commercial broadcaster's nonsubscription streams in 2026, ephemeral copies included. It rises $0.0001 a year to $0.0032 in 2030.
0.0028 dollars per performance, commercial broadcasters, 2026
nbr-number-webcasters-2025
Commercial webcasters' nonsubscription rate per performance, 2025
The 2025 nonsubscription rate in 37 CFR 380.10; subscription services paid $0.0032. The section showed no 2026 rate on 18 November 2026.
0.0025 dollars per performance, commercial webcasters, 2025
nbr-note-web6-status
Web VI: no final rule for section 380.10 webcasters found as of 20 November 2026
Four Web VI final rules for 2026 to 2030 were published on 10 March 2026. None for the webcasters in 37 CFR 380.10 was found as of 20 November 2026.
nbr-mistake-rate-artist-pay
Mistake: reading a per-performance rate as what an artist is paid
A rate such as $0.0028 is what a service owes for one performance. The collective then divides it between owners, featured artists and the non-featured funds.
nbr-note-rome-wppt
Rome and the WPPT provide a payment right for broadcast use that countries may limit
Both WIPO treaties provide one equitable payment when commercial recordings are broadcast or communicated to the public, and both let a country limit it or opt out.
nbr-note-ppl-qualify
PPL pays a performer only for a 'qualifying performance'
A UK performer claim has to pass a test based on where the performance took place or where the performer lives or is a citizen.
nbr-note-sx-national-treatment
SoundExchange's view: some countries pay US creators less because of nationality
SoundExchange's advocacy page says countries such as the UK, France and Japan treat US creators worse on nationality grounds, citing unpaid AM/FM play abroad as an example.
nbr-note-sx-international
SoundExchange can collect abroad for members who sign an international mandate
SoundExchange says members who complete an international mandate can have it collect neighbouring rights money abroad through its agreements with foreign societies.
nbr-note-gvl
GVL handles German neighbouring rights; its foreign service needs an assignment
GVL is the German society for performers and sound recording producers. For performers, its international service needs an agreement that transfers international rights to GVL.
nbr-table-societies
Recording societies SoundExchange lists as partners in this guide's countries
Built from SoundExchange's partner list, which marks whether each agreement covers performers, rights owners or both. Only PPL's and GVL's own pages were read for this guide.
nbr-note-cid-eligibility
Content ID is for owners with exclusive rights to a large body of material
YouTube approves Content ID only for owners holding exclusive rights to a large catalogue of original material that is uploaded often, and who show a need.
nbr-mistake-cid-reference
Mistake: sending a full album, remaster or non-exclusive track as a Content ID reference
References must be exclusive, distinct and given one per piece. YouTube lists full albums, remasters and non-exclusive licences as ineligible.
nbr-checklist-recording-money
Recording income checklist
Tick what applies to you. Each register is separate, and a lawyer should read any agreement that assigns rights.
unc-term-unmatched
Unmatched royalties

Money collected for a use of a song that cannot be paid yet because the song, its owner or the owner's share is still unknown or unfound. In US law it means the owner "has not been identified or located".
unc-term-unclaimed
Unclaimed royalties

A loose word for royalties that no owner has collected yet. Meanings vary between collectors, and the MLC uses it both for its wider unclaimed accrued royalties and for one part of them. Read each collector's own definition.
unc-term-black-box
Black box
Informal industry name for a pool of collected royalties that nobody has been able to allocate. It is a nickname, not a legal or official term; collectives use names such as suspense account.
unc-term-suspense-account
Suspense account

An account where a collective holds royalties while the works in a usage report are still unidentified. A 2020 survey for the US Copyright Office lists checking it against past payouts among some societies' pre-payment steps.
unc-note-matching-causes
The commonest reason money goes unmatched is a thin usage report
In a 2020 survey, collectives put first a service report that names the recording but says nothing about the song, its writers or its publishers.
unc-note-conflicting-data
Conflicting registrations and unknown shares hold money back
Money can stay unpaid when registrations disagree, when shares are unknown or add up to more than 100 percent, or when owners dispute a song.
unc-note-foreign-gaps
A song can be known at home and missing abroad
A collective may lack a foreign owner's details, or hold incomplete data from a sister society, so income earned abroad can stall.
unc-mistake-stale-details
Letting contact and bank details go stale
Collectives surveyed in 2020 listed missing current addresses and bank details among the reasons a known owner still goes unpaid.
unc-note-no-perfect-match
No collective matches everything
The 2020 survey says any claimed 100 percent match rate should be doubted. Its author reports that executives see the high 80s percent as very good for current service reports.
unc-note-statute-public-list
US law makes the MLC list unmatched works and give notice
The statute requires a public place to see unmatched works and claim them, and industry notice of a payout at least 90 days ahead.
unc-table-soundexchange-lists
SoundExchange's four status lists for unclaimed royalties
SoundExchange sorts creators it holds unclaimed royalties for into four lists. The list you are on shows what is missing. How to register and claim is in the claimable-royalties table.
unc-step-ppl
In myPPL, the role you claim decides whether a UK performance pays
When you ask PPL to add you to a recording's line-up, you pick a role. Audible contributions generally count; some studio roles with no audible part do not pay.
unc-note-society-lists
Societies post lists of unidentified works, but not always openly
Posting lists of unidentified works is a common outreach step, but some societies list only works above a money threshold, and some open the lists to members or affiliates only.
unc-note-cmo-matching
Collectives match in layers, and spend manual effort where money is
Societies match by machine first, then research by hand, and some keep manual research for works above a money or usage level, such as $10.
unc-note-identifiers
Identifiers let a collective link your song to you
Collectives use the ISWC for the song, the IPI number for each writer and publisher, and the ISRC for the recording to link a usage report to a payee.
unc-table-undistributed-methods
What collectives do with royalties they cannot allocate
The 2020 survey lists ways societies share out money they cannot allocate, now or in the past. Practice varies by society and by type of income, so ask your own.
unc-note-no-market-share
Most societies surveyed in 2020 did not use US-style market share
Collectives surveyed in 2020 most often did not share out unclaimed money by each owner's market share, the method US law sets for the MLC.
unc-note-social-cultural
Some societies deduct for cultural and social funds
The author of the 2020 survey writes that most societies in continental Europe and Latin America deduct part of collections for social, cultural or educational purposes.
unc-note-study-held-owners
US study: hold money for an owner who is known but cannot be found
The Copyright Office's July 2021 report recommends that the MLC keep holding unclaimed royalties for an owner who is known but cannot be found, until that owner turns up.
unc-step-gather-documents
Gather identity and ownership papers before you claim
Collectives may ask for your legal name and aliases, contact and tax details, proof of identity, and proof of ownership or splits for each work.
unc-mistake-one-registration
Assuming one registration covers every collector
A performing rights society, the MLC and SoundExchange each keep their own accounts. Each pays only what it collects, so a missing registration leaves money unclaimed.
unc-note-deadlines
Do not assume a deadline, and do not assume time is unlimited
The CMRRA, PPL and SoundExchange pages checked here name no claim deadline. That does not mean money waits forever, and the MLC's April 2027 date is a start, not a cut-off.
unc-checklist-unclaimed
Unclaimed-money check, step by step
A short pass to find money held for you, built from each collector's own page and the 2020 survey for the US Copyright Office.
unc-number-notice-days
Minimum notice before a US unclaimed distribution
Section 115 makes the MLC publicize any pending distribution of unclaimed money across the industry at least this many days before it is paid.
90 days' minimum notice before an MLC unclaimed distribution
unc-number-cisac-music
Music collections by CISAC member societies in 2025
Scale only: gross, before deductions, from CISAC's 2026 report. Up 11.9% on 2024, or 5.3% without The MLC, new in 2025. Not an unclaimed total.
14.06 EUR billion, gross, 2025
unc-number-ppl-tracks
Tracks on PPL's repertoire database
PPL says its repertoire database holds over 28 million tracks. Members search it for recordings they performed on before they claim.
28 million tracks or more
ai-note-human-authorship
US copyright needs a human author, and the courts have said so
In the US, a work with no human author cannot be registered, and the Supreme Court declined in March 2026 to revisit that.
ai-note-prompts-alone
A text prompt alone does not make you the author of the output
The Copyright Office says that, with today's tools, prompts alone do not give a user enough control to be the author of what comes back.
ai-step-register-ai-material
Registering a song that contains AI material with the US Copyright Office
Use the Standard Application, claim only your own authorship, and exclude AI material that is more than a minor part of the work.
ai-note-uk-computer-generated
UK law still protects computer-generated works, but the government proposes ending that
Section 9(3) of the UK Act names the person who arranged a computer-generated work as its author; the March 2026 report proposes removing that rule.
ai-note-part3-training
The Copyright Office's training report exists only as a pre-publication version
Part 3 calls training an audio model to make new recordings for the same market at best modestly transformative, and leaves fair use to case-by-case decisions.
ai-note-eu-reservation
In the EU, rightsholders can reserve their music from commercial text and data mining
In the EU, commercial text and data mining of lawfully accessible works is allowed unless the rightsholder reserves the use; German law requires online reservations to be machine-readable.
ai-note-gpai-duties
EU rules make AI model providers keep a copyright policy and publish a training summary
In the EU, general-purpose AI model providers must keep a copyright policy and publish a training summary; Commission enforcement, with fines, began on 2 August 2026.
ai-term-tdm
Text and data mining (TDM)

Automated analysis of one or more digital works to extract information such as patterns, trends and correlations. In the EU, a commercial use is allowed only where the rightsholder has not reserved it.
ai-term-training-summary
Training content summary
The overview of what content trained a general-purpose AI model, which EU rules require its provider to publish in the Commission's template format.
ai-term-digital-replica
Digital replica

In the NO FAKES bill (S. 4591, not law as of November 2026), a newly made, computer-generated, highly realistic copy of a person's voice or likeness. Authorised remixes, samples and remasters are excluded.
ai-note-elvis-act
Tennessee's ELVIS Act protects a person's voice, including a simulated one
Since 1 July 2024, Tennessee law covers a voice whether real or simulated, and reaches tools whose main purpose is copying one person's voice.
ai-note-ca-ny-replicas
California and New York have signed performer digital replica laws
Governors signed California bills on 17 September 2024 and New York bills on 11 December 2025; read the statute text before relying on a summary.
ai-note-no-fakes-status
The NO FAKES Act has cleared a Senate committee but is not law
S. 4591 is a bill, not law. It was reported to the Senate on 24 June 2026 (Calendar No. 446); no Senate or House vote was found as of 20 November 2026.
ai-note-no-fakes-content
What the reported NO FAKES text would do for a voice or likeness
The reported bill would create a federal property right in voice and visual likeness, with limits on licence length and a takedown process for platforms.
ai-mistake-broad-voice-licence
Mistake: signing a long or total voice and likeness licence without a music lawyer
A broad licence of your voice or likeness can leave you without control for years; both the Copyright Office and the NO FAKES text point to that risk.
ai-mistake-voice-clone
Mistake: releasing a voice clone of a real artist without their approval
Spotify allows vocal impersonation only with the impersonated artist's authorisation, and Tennessee law can reach unauthorised voice use.
ai-note-gema-openai
In Germany, a court ruled for GEMA against OpenAI over song lyrics
Munich Regional Court I ruled for GEMA on 11 November 2025 (42 O 14139/24); LTO reported it was not yet final.
ai-note-gema-suno
In Germany, a court largely upheld GEMA's claims against Suno
Per the court's own release, Munich Regional Court I largely upheld GEMA's claims against Suno on 31 July 2026 (42 O 763/25); the judgment is not final.
ai-note-labels-suno
UMG and Sony v Suno: two US cases, each an allegation so far
UMG and Sony's claims against Suno in D. Mass. are allegations; Suno's answer of 1 September 2026 admits it took audio data from YouTube for its training set.
ai-note-sony-udio
Sony v Udio: two New York cases, and UMG settled
Sony's claims against Udio (S.D.N.Y.) are allegations; Udio's answer of 27 August 2026 admits it took audio data from YouTube for its training set.
ai-note-concord-anthropic
Concord v Anthropic: the publishers moved to drop two claims in April 2026
In the first lyrics case against Anthropic, the publishers filed notice on 20 April 2026 dropping two secondary-liability claims with prejudice; a second case is pending.
ai-note-indie-class-actions
Independent artists have proposed class actions against Suno and Udio
Trade press reports Justice v Suno largely survived a motion to dismiss on 20 August 2026, and Woulard v Udio moved to New York on 3 August 2026.
ai-note-socan-suno
SOCAN says it has sued Suno over 150 outputs
SOCAN sued Suno in the Federal Court of Canada (T-3803-26) over a sample of 150 outputs; it says Suno has neither a licence nor paid it. The claims are unproven.
ai-table-tracker
Tracker: pending AI and rights matters, with the date of the latest step found
Status as of 20 November 2026. Allegations are not findings; check the court or official page for anything newer.
ai-note-label-publisher-deals
Labels and publishers have licensed AI music firms since October 2025
UMG, Merlin, Warner, Kobalt and BMG have announced AI deals; none of the sources opened gives money terms, and some rest on trade reports.
ai-note-gema-licence-model
GEMA's AI licence model asks for 30 percent of a provider's net income
GEMA's two-part licence model, set out in September 2024, asks AI providers for a 30 percent share of net income, with a minimum royalty tied to output.
ai-note-stim-licence
Sweden's STIM announced a collective AI licence in September 2025
CISAC reported on 9 September 2025 that STIM signed what it called the first collective AI licence, with attribution technology built in.
ai-note-socan-musical-ai
SOCAN named Musical AI an approved attribution partner
SOCAN's release of 20 July 2026 sets opt-in and credit-and-compensation principles; it gives no rates or payout terms.
ai-note-art50-labelling
EU AI-content labelling duties apply from 2 August 2026
In the EU, AI Act transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026, and a voluntary code on marking and labelling AI content was finalised on 10 June 2026.
ai-note-art50-grace
In the EU, AI generators already on sale have until 2 December 2026 to mark outputs
In the EU, AI systems generating synthetic audio and placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must meet the Article 50(2) marking duty by 2 December 2026.
ai-note-uk-report
The UK dropped the opt-out data mining exception as its preferred route
The UK government's report of 18 March 2026 no longer prefers a wide data mining exception with an opt-out, and says it will not reform copyright until it is confident.
ai-note-spotify-ai
Spotify's AI policy: no unauthorised voice clones, a spam filter and AI credits
Spotify's post of 25 September 2025 bars vocal impersonation without the artist's approval and backs AI credits delivered through DDEX.
ai-number-deezer-uploads
Deezer says AI tracks passed 50 percent of daily uploads at the June 2026 peak
Deezer's own detector count: about 90,000 fully AI tracks a day, not independently checked. The release dates its first AI tagging to both June 2025 and June 2026.
Over 50 percent of new uploads at the June 2026 peak
ai-number-deezer-streams
Deezer says fully AI tracks are 1 to 3 percent of its streams
Deezer's own figure, as of June 2026. It excludes detected AI tracks from recommendations and says up to 85% of their 2025 streams were fraudulent.
1 to 3 percent of Deezer streams
ai-note-youtube-ai
YouTube requires disclosure of realistic AI content and offers face likeness detection
YouTube requires creators to disclose realistic AI-made content, including music that is the main focus of a video; its likeness tool described matches faces.
ai-note-apple-distributors
Apple Music's AI tags depend on what labels and distributors declare
Music Business Worldwide reports Apple's four AI transparency tags rely on suppliers; CD Baby says it is working on AI credits with Spotify.
ai-note-ddex-ai-flags
DDEX ERN 4.3.1 can mark a recording or contribution as made by generative AI
Version 4.3.1 of the DDEX release message adds ways to say a recording, or one contribution, was made fully or partly by a generative AI tool.
ai-note-pro-alignment
ASCAP, BMI and SOCAN accept partly AI works and reject wholly AI ones
On 28 October 2025 the three societies aligned: works that combine AI material with human authorship can be registered, entirely AI-made works cannot.
ai-note-mlc-ai
The MLC will not register wholly AI works and does not judge individual songs
The MLC follows Copyright Office guidance, cannot register entirely AI-generated works and does not decide whether a given song has enough human authorship.
ai-note-gema-declaration
GEMA's work form has a box confirming the work was not made only by AI
GEMA's online work registration has a tick box confirming the work was not made only by AI, added as part of its anti-fraud work.
ai-term-ai-assisted
AI-assisted work and AI-generated output
SOCAN's split: an AI-assisted work is made by a person using AI as a tool; an AI-generated output is made with minimal human involvement and cannot be registered.
ai-checklist-use-ai
If you use AI in your music
A working list for a songwriter, artist, producer or admin who uses AI tools. It is not legal advice; ask a music lawyer about contracts.
claim-april-2027-claim-deadline
Do I have to claim my unclaimed MLC royalties before April 2027?
No. April 2027 is when the MLC plans to start paying out remaining unclaimed accrued royalties by market share. It is a start date, not a cut-off for claims.
Not supported
claim-mlc-fee
Does the MLC take a fee from my mechanical royalties?
No. The MLC says it deducts no fees from the mechanical royalties it pays out. Digital services fund its budget separately. Your own publisher or administrator may still keep a share.
Not supported
claim-copyright-registration-mlc
Does registering my song with the Copyright Office also register it with the MLC?
No. The Copyright Office says a copyright registration does not replace an MLC registration. You, or your publisher or administrator, still have to register the song with the MLC.
Not supported
claim-fixed-streaming-rate
Does a streaming service pay a fixed mechanical rate per stream?
No. US law sets no per-stream amount for mechanicals. It sets a formula that produces a pool for each service offering, which is then divided across plays.
Not supported
claim-131-cents-streaming
Is 13.1 cents the streaming mechanical rate?
No. 13.1 cents is the 2026 US rate per work for physical copies and permanent downloads. Streaming mechanicals come from a formula, not that figure.
Not supported
claim-publisher-share-unclaimed
Must publishers pay songwriters a share of unclaimed MLC money they receive?
Yes. A copyright owner that receives an MLC unclaimed distribution must pay or credit its songwriters by reported usage, never less than half of what it receives for their works.
Holds up
claim-black-box
Is a "black box" the same as unclaimed royalties?
Not exactly. Black box is an informal nickname for money no one has allocated. The MLC uses its own terms, and each collector defines its own.
Depends
claim-pro-covers-everything
Does registering with my PRO also get me SoundExchange or MLC money?
No. A performing rights society, the MLC and SoundExchange each keep their own accounts and pay only what they collect. Each needs its own registration.
Not supported
claim-worldwide-market-share
Do collecting societies worldwide share out unclaimed money by market share?
Not as a rule. US law tells the MLC to use market share. A 2020 survey of collectives found most of those taking part did not use owner market share for such money.
Overstated
claim-master-owns-song
Does owning the master mean I own the song?
No. The song and the recording are two separate works with separate rights, and they can have different owners.
Not supported
claim-featured-artists-45
Are featured artists paid 45% of US digital performance royalties?
It depends on the money. For receipts under the US statutory licence, the law gives featured artists 45 percent, paid per recording. Other income follows contracts.
Depends
claim-registration-to-own
Do I have to register my recording with the Copyright Office to have a copyright?
No. For a US sound recording made since 1978, protection starts when it is fixed. Registration is a separate, optional step with its own form, fee and deposit.
Not supported
claim-am-fm-recording-owner
Do recording owners get paid when a song plays on US AM/FM radio?
Not under US copyright law. Recording owners hold a performance right only for digital audio transmissions, and over-the-air radio broadcasts fall outside it.
Not supported
claim-w8ben-non-us
Do non-US songwriters need to fill in Form W-8 BEN?
It depends on the payer and your situation. The IRS says a foreign individual gives the form to the withholding agent or payer when asked for it.
Depends
